lead: MSK sends bits as two frequencies that are only half a bit rate apart, with phase that never jumps. That makes the envelope constant and the spectrum tidy. GMSK passes the data through a Gaussian lowpass filter before the MSK modulator. The filter narrows the spectrum further but smears each bit into its neighbours. GSM uses GMSK; Bluetooth and some satellite links use related schemes. MSK and GMSK matter when a cheap nonlinear amplifier must send a compact spectrum.
prereq: You need: 6.1 FSK for tone spacing and 6.4 QPSK for the I/Q view.

blocks.text: MSK is continuous-phase FSK with modulation index 0.5. Let R<sub>b</sub> be the bit rate in bits per second and T<sub>b</sub> = 1/R<sub>b</sub> the bit duration in seconds. The two transmitted frequencies are f<sub>c</sub> − Δf and f<sub>c</sub> + Δf, where f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier in Hz and Δf is the peak frequency deviation in Hz. The modulation index is h = 2Δf/R<sub>b</sub>.

blocks.where: h is the modulation index (dimensionless); Δf is the peak frequency deviation in Hz; R<sub>b</sub> is the bit rate in bit/s.

blocks.text: For MSK h = 0.5. Then 2Δf = R<sub>b</sub>/2, so the tone spacing is R<sub>b</sub>/2 and Δf = R<sub>b</sub>/4. The phase changes by ±πh = ±π/2 over each bit. That phase never jumps at a bit boundary: it is continuous. The envelope stays constant. The spacing is the smallest that keeps the two tones orthogonal over one bit; some syllabi call MSK fast FSK.
s(t) = A [ I(t) cos(πt/(2T<sub>b</sub>)) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) − Q(t) sin(πt/(2T<sub>b</sub>)) sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) ]
blocks.where: s(t) is the transmitted signal; A is the amplitude; f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier in Hz; T<sub>b</sub> is the bit duration in s; I(t) and Q(t) are ±1 data streams offset by T<sub>b</sub>; the sine and cosine factors are half-sinusoid pulse weights of length 2T<sub>b</sub>.

blocks.text: This is OQPSK with sinusoidal pulse weighting. The I and Q streams are offset by T<sub>b</sub>, so their transitions do not coincide.

items: VCO generation: the data drives a voltage-controlled oscillator between f<sub>c</sub> − Δf and f<sub>c</sub> + Δf. The oscillator phase is continuous by construction.
I/Q generation: split the bits into even and odd streams, delay Q by T<sub>b</sub>, multiply by the half-sine weights, modulate cos and sin carriers, and add.

blocks.text: Coherent detection mixes the received signal with cos and sin carriers, lowpass filters the two outputs, samples at the bit instants, and decides I and Q. A limiter-discriminator can detect MSK non-coherently, but coherent I/Q detection gives better error performance. The constant envelope allows a nonlinear power amplifier.

sections.h3: GMSK: Gaussian filter and the BT product

blocks.text: GMSK adds a Gaussian lowpass filter before the MSK modulator. The filter has a 3 dB bandwidth B Hz. With bit duration T<sub>b</sub> s, the BT product is BT = B T<sub>b</sub>. For a given BT, B = (BT)/T<sub>b</sub> = (BT) R<sub>b</sub>.

blocks.where: B is the Gaussian filter 3 dB bandwidth in Hz; T<sub>b</sub> is the bit duration in s; R<sub>b</sub> = 1/T<sub>b</sub> is the bit rate in bit/s; BT is dimensionless.

blocks.text: Smaller BT gives a narrower spectrum and lower sidelobes. It also gives a longer filter impulse response, so each bit leaks into its neighbours and ISI grows. BT = 0.3 is a common value. The Gaussian pulse is not a Nyquist pulse, so the samples at the receiver are not ISI-free.

GMSK keeps a constant envelope because the filter is before the phase modulator. The filter does not increase the data rate by itself. It trades bandwidth for ISI. A receiver may use matched filters and symbol-by-symbol decisions, or a Viterbi/MLSE detector to handle the ISI.

figure.caption: Data passes through a Gaussian lowpass filter with BT = 0.3, then an MSK modulator with h = 0.5. Note that the filter is before the modulator, so the output GMSK keeps a constant envelope.

examples.question: A GMSK system has bit rate R<sub>b</sub> = 270.833 kbps and BT = 0.3. For MSK, h = 0.5. Find the peak frequency deviation Δf, the tone spacing 2Δf, and the Gaussian filter 3 dB bandwidth B. Use T<sub>b</sub> = 1/R<sub>b</sub>.
steps: Convert the bit rate: R<sub>b</sub> = 270.833 kbps = 270.833 × 10<sup>3</sup> bit/s. Then T<sub>b</sub> = 1/(270.833 × 10<sup>3</sup>) = 3.6923 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s.
Find the peak deviation: Δf = h R<sub>b</sub>/2 = 0.5 × 270.833 × 10<sup>3</sup> / 2 = 67.708 × 10<sup>3</sup> Hz = 67.708 kHz.
Tone spacing: 2Δf = 2 × 67.708 kHz = 135.416 kHz. Check: 2Δf = h R<sub>b</sub> = 0.5 × 270.833 kHz = 135.416 kHz.
Gaussian filter bandwidth: B = (BT) R<sub>b</sub> = 0.3 × 270.833 × 10<sup>3</sup> = 81.250 × 10<sup>3</sup> Hz = 81.25 kHz.
examples.answer: Δf = 67.708 kHz, tone spacing 2Δf = 135.416 kHz, and B = 81.25 kHz.
examples.check:
Rb = 270.833e3
h = 0.5
BT = 0.3
delta_f = h * Rb / 2
spacing = 2 * delta_f
B = BT * Rb
print(round(delta_f / 1e3, 3))
print(round(spacing / 1e3, 3))
print(round(B / 1e3, 3))

traps: Using h = 1 for MSK. MSK has h = 0.5; ordinary BFSK with phase jumps is not MSK.
Confusing peak deviation Δf with tone spacing 2Δf. For MSK, Δf = R<sub>b</sub>/4 and 2Δf = R<sub>b</sub>/2.
Putting the Gaussian filter after the modulator. GMSK filters the data before the MSK modulator, which keeps the envelope constant.
Saying a smaller BT raises the data rate or lowers error probability. Smaller BT narrows the spectrum but adds ISI.
Using B as the bit rate. B is the Gaussian filter 3 dB bandwidth; B = BT × R<sub>b</sub>.

quiz.q: Define the modulation index h of CPFSK in terms of peak deviation and bit rate.
quiz.a: h = 2Δf/R<sub>b</sub>, where Δf is peak deviation in Hz and R<sub>b</sub> is bit rate in bit/s.

quiz.q: What is the tone spacing of MSK in terms of R<sub>b</sub>?
quiz.a: 2Δf = R<sub>b</sub>/2, so the two tones are R<sub>b</sub>/2 apart.

quiz.q: Why does MSK have a constant envelope?
quiz.a: The frequency changes between two values while the phase stays continuous; the amplitude is not switched, so the envelope is constant. This permits nonlinear amplifiers.

quiz.q: An MSK system has R<sub>b</sub> = 64 kbps and h = 0.5. Find Δf and the tone spacing.
quiz.a: Δf = hR<sub>b</sub>/2 = 0.5 × 64/2 = 16 kHz. Tone spacing = 2Δf = 32 kHz.

quiz.q: A GMSK system has R<sub>b</sub> = 100 kbps and BT = 0.3. Find B.
Explain the effect of reducing BT from 0.5 to 0.3 in GMSK.
quiz.a: The spectrum becomes narrower with lower sidelobes. The Gaussian impulse response becomes longer, so ISI increases. The envelope stays constant. The receiver needs better equalization or MLSE to keep the error rate low.

MSK uses h = 0.5, continuous phase, and orthogonal tones spaced R<sub>b</sub>/2. Ordinary BFSK may switch oscillators and jump in phase, which widens the spectrum. MSK has a more compact spectrum and constant envelope.

beyond: Not for the exam. GMSK is the modulation of GSM, so its BT = 0.3 choice links filter design to adjacent-channel interference. Newer systems often use OFDM or filtered OFDM, which move pulse shaping to the subcarrier level. GMSK receivers can use Laurent decomposition to represent the signal as a sum of pulse-amplitude components. Search terms: Gaussian pulse shaping, Laurent decomposition, MLSE receiver for GMSK, spectral efficiency of MSK.
